2. Ascomycetes (Sac fungi) Characteristics features of ascomycetes are as follows:
a. They are commonly known as sac-fungi due to presence of special sac like structure called ascus.
b. Most of them are terrestrial and occur as saprophyte or parasite.
Biology, Grade 11 | 89
c. They are multicellular, mycelium consists of septate hyphae but yeast is unicellular. Septa possess central pores.
d. There is completely absence of motile structure in the life cycle. e. Asexual reproduction takes place by conidia produced by conidiophores. Conidia on

germination produce mycelium. f. Sexual reproduction takes place by sexual spores called as ascospores produced in ascus. g. Asci may occur freely or grouped to form definite multicellular structure of fruiting body called ascocarp. Examples: Saccharomyces(yeast), Pencillium, Aspergillus, Claviceps, Neurospora, etc.
a. Saccharomycetes (Yeast)
b. Aspergillus
Fig: 2.4.2 Ascomycetes
3. Basidiomycetes (Club fungi) Characteristics features of basidiomycetes are as follows:
a. They are found in soil, on logs and tree stumps and in living plant bodies as parasites. b. Mycelium are filamentous, branched and septate hyphae. Each septum consist of

pore called dolipore. c. Mycelium are of two types: primary mycelium and secondary mycelium. d. Primary mycelium is monokaryotic, develops from the germination of basidiospores. e. Secondary mycelium is long lived and septate. They are dikaryotic, and formed by the fusion of primary mycelia. f. Vegetative reproduction take place by fragmentation but the asexual spores are generally not found. g. The dikaryotic cell is formed during sexual reproduction. Examples: Agaricus (Mushroom), Ustilago (smut), Puccinia, etc.
a. Agaricus
b. Ustilago Fig: 2.4.3 Basidiomycetes

4. Deuteromycetes (Fungi imperfecti) Characteristics features of deuteromycetes are as follows:
a. They are commonly known as imperfect fungi because only the asexual or vegetative phases of these fungi are known.

b. They are saprophytes or parasites. c. The mycelium consists of well developed, branched and septate hyphae. d. Asexual reproduction takes place by the formation of conidia. e. Sexual reproduction is absent.
Examples: Alternaria, Trichoderma Alternaria, Cladosporium, etc.
a. Alternaria
b. Trichoderma Fig: 2.4.4 Deuteromycetes
2.2.3 MUCOR
Systematic Position Kingdom Division Class Order Family Genus
: Mycota : Zygomycota : Phycomycetes : Mucorales : Muroraceae : Mucor
Occurrence It is commonly known as black mould or bread mould. They are saprophytic and occur on bread, jam, jelly, cheese, pickle, leather, cattle dung, food stuffs and soil rich in humus.

Morphology The vegetative bodies of Mucor consist of long, cylindrical, branched, coenocytic hyphae. The group of hyphae is known as mycelium. Mycelium consists of three types of hyphae: a. Submerged/sub-terranean hyphae: They are highly branched, smaller and penetrate the substratum spreading inside the body of substratum. They help in absorption of nutrients and fixation. b. Prostrate hyphae: They are highly branched and spread in all direction on the surface of substratum that helps to fix to the substratum. c. Aerial hyphae: They are aerial hyphae growing vertically from the prostate hyphae. They bear sporangia at its tip so it is also known as sporangiophore. They help in asexual reproduction.
Biology, Grade 11 | 91

Figure 2.4.5 Morphology of vegetative body of Mucor Reproduction Mucor reproduce by vegetative, asexual and sexual method. 1. Vegetative reproduction: It takes place by fragmentation. During unfavourable condition the hyphae are fragmented mechanically or by decay. On return of favourable condition, these fragments develop into new mycelium. 2. Asexual Reproduction: Asexual reproduction takes place by non-motile structure known as sporangiospores, chlamydospores and oidia, a. Sporangiospores or spores: The reproduction by sporangiophore takes place during favourable condition. The spores are produced inside the sporangia which develop at the apices of special erect aerial hyphae called sporangiophores. The sporangium consists of two distinct region-the outer fertile region called sporangial proper and inner dome shaped sterile region called columella. The nuclei of sporangial proper divide mitotically for several times and form number of multinucleated sporangiospore.
Biology, Grade 11 | 92

Figure 2.4.6 Reproduction by sporangiospore in Mucor After maturation, the columella swells and the sporangial wall burst so the sporangiospores are liberated out. On reaching a suitable substratum, they germinate to give rise to new mycelium.
